summary.one_line: A single-plant Goa maker of polymer compounds for cables and pipeline coatings, raising Rs.255 cr of fresh capital. It has delevered and its margins have improved sharply, but about 45% of pre-tax profit comes from discretionary vendor discounts, the growth is increasingly low-value resin trading, a promoter-group trader is now a large counterparty, and the company has no moat beyond customer approvals.
bull_points: 100% fresh issue with no offer for sale: all of the up-to-Rs.255 cr goes into the company, mainly Rs.77.56 cr of Goa capex and Rs.89.50 cr of working capital (S1, S3).
Margins expanded sharply over three years: EBITDA margin rose from 7.10% (FY24) to 13.33% (FY26) and 15.15% (Q1 FY27), and PAT went from Rs.7.52 cr to Rs.27.01 cr (S1).
The balance sheet has delevered: debt-to-equity fell from 2.05 (FY24) to 0.56 (FY26), and borrowings fell from Rs.93.77 cr to Rs.51.72 cr (S1, S3).
Enlistment with government agencies and CPSEs and a pre-approved product portfolio give some stickiness: 96.51% of FY26 revenue came from repeat customers (S1, S8).
Its end markets (power, telecom, railway, water and gas pipelines) are growing. CRISIL sizes Indian polymer compounding at USD 9,934 mn in 2025, growing about 9% a year to 2031 (S1).
bear_points: Profit depends on supplier generosity: vendor trade discounts were about Rs.16.26 cr in FY26, or 45% of PBT, after 59% in FY25 and 74% in FY24, and they are discretionary (S9, S23).
One supplier provided about 72% of FY26 raw material purchases and the top 10 about 94%, mostly without long-term agreements (S8, S23, S19).
Trading rose from about 14% of revenue in FY24 to about 32% in FY26, while manufactured sales fell from roughly Rs.254-255 cr to Rs.237-238 cr (S12, S19, S14).

Purchases from promoter-group trader Vinsul Makardi, which is in a similar line of business, jumped from about Rs.1.5 cr (FY25) to Rs.32.35 cr (FY26). The CMD has personally guaranteed its loans, and there is no non-compete (S20, S18).
Customer concentration has risen: the top 10 customers went from 50.52% of revenue (FY24) to 66.81% (FY26), and the top 5 to 53.45% (S1).
watch_points: Operating cash flow: aggregator tables show positive OCF in FY24-FY26 but -Rs.4.08 cr in Q1 FY27, while the RHP's own risk factor refers to negative operating cash flows in all four periods. This could not be reconciled without the full RHP (S1, S6, S8).
Whether the margin gains hold if vendor discounts shrink. Q1 FY27 raw material cost per tonne jumped to Rs.1,13,065 from Rs.84,959 in FY26 (S1).
Execution of the 148% capacity expansion to 87,301 MTPA: commercial production is targeted for March 2028 and most machines were not yet ordered as of the RHP (S10).
Legacy governance items: untraceable or incorrect corporate records, past Companies Act non-compliances, and 46 untraceable shareholders (S1, S16).

reasoning: The quality of the profit growth is weak. About 45% of FY26 PBT (and 59% and 74% in the two prior years) came from discretionary trade discounts, granted mostly by a supplier base where one vendor supplies about 72% of inputs. The headline margin expansion therefore depends heavily on terms the company does not control (S9, S23, S8).

The growth is not in the manufacturing the IPO money funds. Revenue grew only 10.82% and 6.39% in FY25-FY26, trading's share rose to about 32%, and manufactured sales fell. Funding a 148% capacity expansion on that base is an execution and demand bet, not a response to a full plant: FY26 output was 23,265 MT against 35,251 MTPA of installed capacity (S1, S12, S10).

There is no real moat. Government and CPSE enlistments are a real but modest qualification barrier. The RHP-based disclosures themselves describe an organised and unorganised industry with low entry barriers, and the listed peers (Kingfa, DDev Plastiks, Plastiblends) are many times larger (S1, S18, S8).

Related-party exposure is growing in a way that matters. Promoter-group trader Vinsul Makardi, in a similar business with no non-compete, became a Rs.32.35 cr supplier in FY26 and owed about Rs.6.46 cr at June 2026, and the CMD personally guarantees its loans (S20, S18).

Governance history needs caution: untraceable or incorrect corporate records, admitted past Companies Act non-compliances, delayed statutory filings, 15 criminal cases filed by the company, and frequent independent-director turnover (S1, S18, S11).

Positives exist but do not offset the above. The issue is all-primary, leverage has fallen to 0.56x, and the auditors raised no qualifications. These make it a business to track for a few quarters of listed disclosure, not one to buy at the IPO (S1, S3).

subsections.title: What BLS Polymers makes and who buys it

blocks.text: BLS Polymers, incorporated in Delhi in 1991, makes multiple grades of custom-formulated polymer compounds. These are the raw material for the sheathing, jacketing and insulation of wires and cables, and for anti-corrosion coating of underground oil, gas and water pipelines (S1). Its products include HDPE, MDPE and LLDPE sheathing compounds, XLPE and HFFR compounds for power and railway cables, PVC compounds, cable-filling compounds, and adhesive coating compounds used in three-layer polyethylene (3LPE) pipe coating (S3, S14, S17). Across these categories it offers about 127 grades (S9, S8).

The customers are mainly wire and cable manufacturers and pipeline-coating companies in India, and to a lesser extent overseas. Sales are mostly to private customers through direct sales, and a significant majority of revenue comes from repeat customers (S1). In the end it serves the telecom, power, railway, water distribution and oil and gas distribution industries (S1). Orders are mostly placed under short-term arrangements rather than long-term contracts (S9), and the company has no firm-commitment agreements with customers (S18).

Wire and cable compounds were 80.49%, 81.59% and 80.93% of revenue in FY24, FY25 and FY26, and 73.20% in Q1 FY27 (S1). The company reports a single operating segment under Ind AS 108 (S1). Exports go to Bangladesh, Egypt, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the UAE, the USA and Zambia, with customers in 13 countries over the period (S1). Exports began in 2024 with Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Egypt (S11).

subsections.title: Manufacturing footprint, capacity and the rise of trading

blocks.text: All manufacturing happens at one plant in Verna Industrial Estate, Goa. It covers about 24,220 sq m and has 11 production lines/machines and an in-house lab, and it is close to Mormugao Port (S3, S16, S8). The company describes nine 'Operating Facilities': this plant, a warehouse in Goa, two warehouses in New Delhi and a godown in Bhiwandi (S1). A seven-member R&D team sits in Goa (S8).

blocks.caption: Installed capacity and utilisation at Goa (MTPA)

blocks.text: PE and XLPE lines ran at about three-quarters utilisation in FY26. PVC barely ran (584 MT produced in FY26) and is being phased out (S10). Total FY26 output was 23,265 MT (S10), but the company bought 34,499 MT of material that year (S1). The gap between tonnes bought and tonnes produced is consistent with a large trading business. This is our inference from the two figures, not an RHP statement.

Trading is now about a third of revenue. Resin and polymer trading reportedly rose from about 14% of revenue in FY24 to about 32% in FY26, while manufactured sales fell from roughly Rs.254-255 cr to Rs.237-238 cr (S12, S19). Swastika Investmart separately cites trading at 32% of FY26 revenue (S14). Reported revenue growth therefore overstates growth in the compounding business that the IPO capex is meant to expand.

subsections.title: Customers, suppliers and how concentrated they are

blocks.caption: Customer concentration (share of revenue from operations)

blocks.text: Customer concentration has risen materially. The top 10 went from about half of revenue to two-thirds in two years (S1), and one analysis of the RHP puts the single largest customer at about 31.7% of revenue (S19). Customer names are not disclosed in the materials we could access. The supply side is even more concentrated. Raw materials were Rs.273.02 cr, or 78.13% of FY26 revenue (S9, S13), the largest supplier provided about 71.7% of FY26 procurement, and the top 10 about 93.5% (S23, S19, S8). There are no long-term agreements with most suppliers (S18, S23).

The operating model is a classic converter: buy petrochemical resins (largely PE grades, with some imports, so crude and currency exposure (S12)), compound them with additives on extruder lines in Goa, and sell to cable makers and pipe coaters on short-term orders and credit terms. Working capital is tied up in receivables and inventory (S18). FY26 inventory was held for 66-85 days depending on the source (S8), and the working-capital cycle was about 110 days (S8).

Supplier dependence goes beyond volume. Trade discounts from raw material vendors were about Rs.16.26 cr in FY26, equal to roughly 45% of PBT. They were 59% of PBT in FY25 and 74% in FY24 (S9, S23). They are discretionary and not backed by contracts (S23), and an RHP-based summary states that recent performance partly reflects 'favourable procurement terms and discretionary vendor discounts' that may not be sustainable (S18).

The CRISIL report commissioned for the RHP puts the Indian polymer compounding market at about USD 5,967 mn in 2019 and USD 9,934 mn in 2025. It projects about 9.0% CAGR over 2026-2031 to about USD 16,507 mn (S1). The DRHP version of the same report (August 2025) had projected an 8.2% CAGR to USD 13,415 mn by 2029 (S15). Demand drivers cited are industrialisation, infrastructure, power-sector expansion, renewable integration, telecom and urbanisation (S1).

This headline market is much broader than what BLS actually sells into. It includes automotive, construction, electronics and agriculture compounds (S1). The relevant niche is cable-insulation and sheathing compounds plus 3LPE coating adhesives, and the materials we could access do not size it separately. Even against the broad market, BLS's FY26 revenue of about Rs.349 cr is a very small share.

items: Demand linkage: wire and cable compounds were about 81% of FY26 sales, so BLS's volumes follow cable-industry capex in power transmission, telecom and railways (S1, S8).

Pipeline linkage: the coating-adhesive business (about 19% of sales) follows oil, gas, city-gas and water pipeline build-out. In 2026 the company disclosed an enlistment with a city gas distribution company for coating materials (S8, S11).
Input linkage: margins move with polymer resin prices, which track crude oil (S9, S1).

blocks.caption: Listed peers named in RHP-based comparisons, FY26 (operating metrics only; no valuation)

blocks.text: The listed peers are DDev Plastiks, which is the most direct cable-compound competitor, Kingfa (engineering-plastic compounds) and Plastiblends (masterbatches) (S8). Kkalpana Industries is also named as a competitor (S8). BLS is the smallest of the group and grew slowest of the three compounders in FY26. Its margin advantage over DDev is partly explained by the vendor discounts discussed above (S9, S23). The RHP-based risk disclosures also say the company competes in an organised and unorganised industry with low barriers to entry (S18).

There is also a competitor inside the promoter family. Group company Vinsul Makardi Limited trades polymers and polymer compounds in a similar line of business, and there is no non-compete agreement with it (S20, S18).

The company's claimed strengths are enlistment with government agencies and a pre-approved product portfolio, diversified applications, long-standing customer relationships, pan-India presence, in-house product development, industry tailwinds and experienced promoters (S1). Of these, only the first is a real barrier. Cable makers supplying power utilities, railways and telecom PSUs often need compound grades that are type-approved by those buyers. That creates switching costs and helps explain the high repeat-customer share of about 96.5% (S8, S9).

BLS does not claim an import-substitution position, a market-share leadership claim or a sole-Indian-maker status in the materials we reviewed. Its scale is a fraction of DDev's or Kingfa's (S8). Its margins depend on supplier discounts rather than proprietary technology (S23). Its own disclosures describe low entry barriers (S18).

Moat verdict: narrow at best. Approvals and long relationships give it some customer stickiness, but this is not a structural moat. Scale, technology and input-cost advantages all sit with larger peers, and a promoter-group trader operates in the same space.

blocks.caption: Restated financial summary (Rs. crore; Q1 FY27 not annualised)

blocks.text: Source: restated financial information summarised in the abridged prospectus (S1), converted from Rs. lakh. On the surface the profit story is impressive. EBITDA more than doubled and PAT rose about 3.6x between FY24 and FY26, driven by gross margin expanding almost 6 percentage points (S1). Revenue growth, though, was modest at 10.82% and then 6.39% (S1).

The margin gains need careful reading. Vendor trade discounts were 74%, 59% and 45% of PBT in FY24, FY25 and FY26 (S23), and about Rs.16.26 cr in FY26 (S9). Without them, FY26 PBT would have been closer to Rs.20 cr than Rs.36 cr (our arithmetic). One RHP-based analysis also notes earnings adjustments, including liability write-backs and a related-party interest waiver, that move PAT by about -2.8% (S19).

Q1 FY27 raw material cost per tonne jumped to Rs.1,13,065 from Rs.84,959 in FY26 (S1), yet gross margin still rose to 23.38% (S1). Whether that comes from pricing power, product mix or more discounts is not explained in the materials we could access.

Balance sheet figures are from S1 and S3. The deleveraging is real: borrowings fell by about Rs.42 cr between FY24 and FY26 while net worth doubled from retained profit (S3, S1). FY25 financing outflow was about Rs.25.7 cr, consistent with debt repayment (S6). Debt rose again to Rs.62.91 cr by June 2026, alongside negative Q1 operating cash flow (S3, S8). Share capital rose from Rs.9.60 cr to Rs.45.03 cr in FY26 (S6). That step-up in issued capital, with reserves falling from Rs.58.34 cr to Rs.49.90 cr (S3), points to a capitalisation of reserves, i.e. a bonus issue. This is our inference.

Operating cash flow figures are inconsistent across sources. Aggregators show positive OCF of Rs.2.68 cr (FY24) and Rs.24.85 cr (FY25) (S6), and about Rs.38.06 cr in FY26 (S8). The FY26 figure is higher than PAT, partly helped by higher supplier payables per one review (S20). Q1 FY27 was negative at Rs.-4.08 cr (S8). Yet risk factor 8 in the RHP, as quoted in the abridged prospectus, says the company has 'experienced negative cash flows in relation to our operating activities' in Q1 FY27 and the last three financial years (S1). Some secondary reviews read this as negative OCF in every year (S21, S18).

We could not reconcile the RHP's negative-operating-cash-flow risk factor with the positive OCF figures on aggregator sites without the full cash flow statement. FY24 OCF of Rs.2.68 cr on Rs.7.52 cr PAT was weak in any case. Treat cash conversion as unproven.

subsections.title: Does the trend support the growth story?

items: Supports it: margin and return-ratio expansion, falling leverage and a clean auditor report. The statutory auditors raised no qualification, reservation or emphasis of matter (S1).
Undercuts it: top-line growth of 6-11% a year, with an increasing share from low-margin resin trading, while manufactured sales fell (S1, S12, S19).
Undercuts it: profit is heavily reliant on discretionary supplier discounts (S23).
Undercuts it: customer concentration rose sharply to 66.81% from the top 10 (S1).
Open question: purchase volume grew from 28,417 MT (FY24) to 34,499 MT (FY26), about 21%, while the plant ran at about 66% overall (S1, S10).

blocks.text: Overall, the financial trend shows a business that has become more profitable and less leveraged, but not one whose core compounding volumes are growing fast enough to justify a 148% capacity build on their own. The equity story rests on future demand and export ramp-up rather than on demonstrated capacity constraints.

sections.title: Issue details and objects of the issue

blocks.caption: Key terms
rows: 100% fresh issue, book built; no offer for sale
Up to 1,70,00,000 equity shares of Rs.10 face value; up to Rs.255 cr at the upper band
Anchor 26 Oct 2026; open 27 Oct; close 29 Oct; allotment 30 Oct; listing (tentative) 3 Nov 2026

blocks.text: Terms are from S1 and S3. The issue was made under Regulation 6(1) of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, and NSE is the designated stock exchange (S1). The DRHP was filed on 6 August 2025 (S15, S22). SEBI observations were received in December 2025 (S26), and the RHP is dated 16 October 2026 and posted on SEBI's public-issues page (S1, S2).
Because there is no OFS, every rupee raised goes to the company, and no promoter is cashing out at the IPO. Promoter ownership is diluted from 98.53% to about 71.53% only by the new shares (S3).

blocks.caption: Use of net proceeds (Rs. crore)
rows: Capex: expansion of the Goa facility (more capacity for existing PE/XLPE products)
To be finalised; capped at 25% of gross proceeds (Rs.63.75 cr max)

blocks.text: Amounts are from the abridged RHP (S1), the DRHP press coverage (S15, S16) and Chittorgarh (S3). Percentages and the residual are our arithmetic. Both earmarked objects grew between the DRHP and the RHP: capex by about Rs.7.7 cr and working capital by Rs.14.5 cr. About two-thirds of the specified use is therefore capacity plus funding receivables and inventory, and no debt repayment is planned from the proceeds (S1).

Capex breakdown: civil works and utilities of Rs.42.92 cr and plant and machinery of Rs.34.63 cr. Rs.11.78 cr had already been deployed by 31 August 2026 (S10). Of the five new machines, one XLPE and one PE machine had been ordered and three were not yet ordered (S10). The expansion uses about 5,748 sq m of unused land within the existing site, so no land acquisition is needed. The cost estimate has not been appraised by a bank or financial institution (S10).

subsections.title: Expansion timeline and what the money buys

blocks.caption: Implementation schedule disclosed in the RHP
rows: to Sep 2027 (start date in RHP summary appears misprinted)

blocks.text: The schedule is per S10. Installed capacity would go from 35,251 to 87,301 MTPA (+52,050 MTPA, +148%), entirely in PE (+29,192) and XLPE (+22,858) (S10). The existing consent to operate covers only 38,400 MTPA, and the company's own projected production by March 2028 is 38,394 MTPA. Pending approvals include building plan, factory layout, consent to operate, factory licence, stability certificate and fire NOC (S10).

The new capacity will not contribute meaningfully before FY29. Even then, the company's own production projection (about 38,400 MT by March 2028) is far below the 87,301 MTPA installed figure (S10). The capex is a long-dated option on demand, not near-term earnings.

blocks.caption: Promoters (pre-issue holding)
rows: Non-executive director since 7 Apr 2025; with the company since incorporation; over 35 years in polymers; MD from Nov 2016 until he resigned that role on 2 Mar 2025
Director of BLS Finvest, B.L. & Sons, Basant India (also CFO there) and several investment companies
Over 29 years in polymer processing; director of B.L. & Sons, BLS Ecotech and others
Director of BLS International Services, BLS E-Services, B.L. & Sons and investment companies
Chairman and MD (term to 19 May 2030); with the company since Sep 2016; oversees manufacturing, product development and exports

blocks.text: Promoter data is from S1 and S11. Promoters hold 66.65% and promoter-group entities a further 31.88%, mostly Aggarwal-family investment companies such as Intime Finance, Fragrance Credit, V.S. Estates and Wonder Rock Finance (S1). The board has six members: Karan Aggarwal (CMD), Dinesh Sharma (executive director, with the company since 1991, handles marketing), Vinod Aggarwal (non-executive), and independent directors Manoj Joshi, Shivani Mishra and Arun Kumar Verma (S1, S11). The CFO is Arvind Kumar Agarwal and the CS is Neha Kumar Sunit (S1).

The family has long industry tenure: three promoters cite 29-35+ years in polymers (S1). Several promoters, however, spend much of their directorship time in group finance and investment companies and in other BLS-group businesses (S1). Day-to-day leadership has recently passed to the 40-year-old Karan Aggarwal (S11). Executive pay is modest: Rs.24 lakh for Karan Aggarwal and Rs.13.14 lakh for Dinesh Sharma in FY26 (S11).

Board churn: two independent directors resigned in April 2025 citing an 'unavoidable personal situation', and another resigned in January 2026 citing a medical condition. Three of the current independents were appointed in 2025-26 (S11). This is not unusual before an IPO, but it means the independent oversight has little track record.

Most of the RPTs are routine. These include an advisory-services agreement with Vinod Aggarwal dated 1 April 2023, and five 11-month leases of premises from Vinod Aggarwal, Karan Aggarwal and family members, with monthly rents from Rs.2,000 to Rs.8.06 lakh (S11). One relationship is not routine.

items: Vinsul Makardi Limited is a group company and promoter-group entity that trades polymers and polymer compounds, a similar line of business, and there is no non-compete agreement with it (S20, S18).
BLS both buys raw material from Vinsul and sells products to it, which Vinsul then resells (S20, S18).
Purchases from Vinsul reportedly rose from about Rs.1.5 cr in FY25 to Rs.32.35 cr in FY26 (S20). One RHP analysis puts these purchases at about 9.3% of revenue (S19).
About Rs.6.46 cr was owed by Vinsul to BLS at 30 June 2026, in a quarter in which BLS made no sales to it (S20).
CMD Karan Aggarwal has personally guaranteed Vinsul's loan facilities. An older filing excerpt also shows a Rs.9 cr letter of comfort given to Vinsul (S18, S20).
An RHP-based analysis also flags a related-party interest waiver among the earnings adjustments (S19).

blocks.text: This is the one RPT investors should not dismiss. A promoter-family trader in the same business has grown into one of the issuer's larger suppliers in a single year, holds a receivable balance, and is backed by the CMD's personal guarantee. That creates room for value to move between the listed company and a family entity. Its size relative to BLS's Rs.36 cr PBT makes it material.

items: Certain corporate records and filings are untraceable or incorrect. Reportedly these include filings from 1991-2013, and the company admits it may face penalties (S1, S16).
There have been past instances of non-compliance with Companies Act, 2013 provisions (S1), and past delays in statutory dues and GST/EPF filings (S18).
46 shareholders holding 3,32,851 shares are untraceable (S1).
The auditors expressed no qualification, reservation, adverse remark or emphasis of matter on the restated period (S1).

blocks.text: Litigation counts are from S1. The litigation load is small in money terms. The 15 criminal cases filed by the company are not described in the abridged prospectus. RHP-based summaries separately mention instances of customer cheque dishonour (S18), which would fit cases filed by a company chasing receivables, but we could not confirm this link. The two criminal matters against directors are not detailed in the materials we could access.

items: 1. Vendor-discount dependence: discretionary trade discounts were about 45% of FY26 PBT (59% FY25, 74% FY24). Losing them would wipe out most of the margin expansion (S23, S9).
2. Single-supplier dependence: about 72% of FY26 raw material came from one supplier and about 94% from the top 10, mostly without long-term agreements (S23, S8).
3. Customer concentration: the top 10 customers were 66.81% of FY26 revenue (50.52% in FY24), the top customer about 31.7%, and orders are short-term (S1, S19, S9).
4. End-market concentration: about 81% of revenue comes from wire and cable compounds, tying BLS to cable-industry capex cycles (S1).

blocks.text: Together these mean a small number of counterparties on both sides of the business decide a large part of BLS's profitability. Many companies have the generic 'raw material price volatility' risk. These specific concentrations are what separate this one from the boilerplate.

The supplier-side risks (items 1 and 2) are the most decision-relevant. If the dominant supplier tightens terms, both input availability and roughly 45% of pre-tax profit are exposed at the same time (S23, S9).

items: 5. Expansion execution: a 148% capacity jump at a single plant, with most machines not yet ordered, several approvals pending, an unappraised cost estimate and commercial production only by March 2028 (S10, S1).
6. Related-party and conflict risk: Vinsul Makardi is a fast-growing related supplier and customer in the same business, with no non-compete and a CMD personal guarantee (S20, S18).

7. Cash conversion: negative operating cash flow in Q1 FY27 (Rs.-4.08 cr), working-capital intensity of about 110 days, and an RHP risk factor citing negative operating cash flows across the review period (S8, S1).
8. Single-site and legacy-compliance risk: all production is in Goa (S8), and there are untraceable records, past Companies Act non-compliances and filing delays (S1, S18).

blocks.text: Risks we consider secondary: export concentration in the Middle East, especially Saudi Arabia (S18, S12), and expansion into regions where the company has little prior presence (S1). Exports were only 5.46% of FY26 revenue (S8), so these are real but small.
The RHP itself describes its capacity and utilisation data as based on 'various assumptions and estimates' (S1). Investors cannot independently confirm how much room the existing plant actually has.
We found no management interview, investor call or analyst meet transcript in news searches. Management's forward statements are limited to the RHP's stated strategies (S1):

items: Add fresh production capacity at the existing Goa facility and broaden the global footprint (S1).
Develop new product categories for wider end-applications (S1).

Deepen penetration in existing international markets and enter new geographies (S1). A service agreement with a UAE marketing/distribution firm covers Egypt, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman and Qatar, but no committed orders are disclosed (S10).
Grow business with existing domestic customers (S1).

blocks.text: The only quantified forward figures are the capex schedule: commercial production of new lines by March 2028, installed capacity of 87,301 MTPA, and projected production of about 38,394 MT by March 2028 (S10). There is no revenue, margin or volume guidance.

Most broker notes recommend subscribing: Swastika, SBI Securities, Religare, BP Equities, Master Capital and Ventura. They cite margin improvement, spare capacity plus expansion, and repeat customers (S14). Several of the same notes flag supplier and customer concentration, raw material volatility, single-plant dependence and whether margins can last (S14). Chittorgarh's tally shows one 'subscribe' and one 'neutral' broker view (S3).

Some of the market commentary questions the timing of a 148% expansion, given slowing revenue growth and roughly two-thirds overall utilisation (S13). We share that concern: the evidence for strong pent-up demand is thin.

Our reading: the company has stated plans, but nothing about the outlook is concrete beyond the capex calendar. Near-term earnings direction will be set by resin prices and vendor-discount terms, not by the new capacity, which arrives in FY28-FY29 at the earliest.

subsections.title: Bids so far (issue still open; closes 29 Oct 2026)

blocks.text: Day 1 data is from S5 and S6. Day 2 data is from S6 and S7, with S8 reporting 35.28x at 7:34 pm. These are partial figures: the issue closes on 29 October, so final numbers are not yet available. Intraday day-2 readings rose from about 11.85x at 10:15 am (S25) to 35.30x by evening (S6). Day-2 bids totalled about 42.0 crore shares against 1.19 crore offered (S6). Some aggregator headlines misstate the day-wise totals (S4), so the table uses the exchange-based category figures.

Anchor book: Rs.76.50 cr was raised on 26 October from 51,00,000 shares at Rs.150, split about 58% to FPIs and 42% to AIFs (S3). Named anchors include Nakshatra Bharat Vantage Fund, Venus Investments VCC, Radiant Global Fund, Pine Oak Global Fund, Vikasa India EIF I Fund and Innovative Vision Fund (S5). None is a large domestic mutual fund. Lock-in: 50% of anchor shares until 29 November 2026 and the rest until 28 January 2027 (S3).

The grey market premium is unofficial, unregulated and inconsistent across trackers. Reported figures range from about Rs.18 (S24) and Rs.20-22 (S14) to about Rs.38 (S8). It is noted here only for completeness and plays no part in our verdict. Oversubscription concentrated in NII and retail does not change the business-quality concerns above.

BLS Polymers IPO Day 2: Subscription Status, Timeline & Key Issue Details
Dhariwal Buildtech, ESDS Software Solution, BLS Polymers Get Sebi Nod to Float IPOs

method: Research was done on 2026-10-28, day 2 of the 3-day issue, so subscription figures are partial. The primary document actually read was the SEBI-hosted abridged prospectus (S1), a 13-page summary of the RHP dated 16 Oct 2026. It supplied the business summary, customer concentration, restated financial summary and KPIs, objects, shareholding, the top-10 risk factors, board/KMP and the litigation table. The full RHP (on Unistone Capital's site) and the full DRHP (NSE archive, S22) could not be read: the RHP exceeded the fetch size limit and the DRHP timed out twice. Detailed RHP disclosures were therefore cross-verified across at least two secondary sources wherever possible, and single-source items are flagged in the text. These cover capacity and utilisation, the capex breakdown and timeline, revenue mix, supplier concentration, vendor trade discounts, trading share of revenue, Vinsul Makardi related-party transactions, peer operating metrics, cash flows and board changes. Material gaps: (1) operating cash flow figures from aggregators (positive OCF FY24-FY26) conflict with the RHP risk factor wording about negative operating cash flows, and this could not be resolved without the full cash flow statement; (2) customer and supplier names, the nature of the 15 criminal cases filed by the company, and the full RPT schedule with exact amounts were not available; (3) the Vinsul Makardi purchase and receivable figures, and the 45/59/74% trade-discount-to-PBT ratios, come from secondary RHP analyses (S20, S23, S9, S19, S18). Some were seen only in search-result snippets because the page returned 403. Source dates are publication dates where shown, otherwise the access date (2026-10-28). Per the brief, valuation (P/E, EV/EBITDA, peer multiples) is deliberately excluded. Grey market premium is reported only as unofficial and inconsistent, and is not used in the verdict. Derived figures (percent of gross proceeds, PBT ex-discounts, bonus-issue inference, purchase-vs-production gap) are our own arithmetic or inference and are labelled as such.
